newsitem.title: CHINA: China cool on Taiwan shipping links deal.
newsitem.headline: China cool on Taiwan shipping links deal.

text.p: China on Thursday played down a deal on adopting direct shipping links with rival Taiwan, while analysts doubted Hong Kong would suffer if the colony's role as lucrative middleman was diminished.

"The suggestions we have made to the Taiwan side (in the past) about direct links have never received a very good or positive reaction," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said at a news briefing.
Non-government negotiators from the two sides, meeting in Hong Kong on Wednesday, reached what they called a consensus on ending a decades-old ban on direct shipping links.
"Some non-government groups and individuals have made many proposals concerning direct links but some of those have not yet been fully implemented," Shen said.
"There have not yet been substantial consultations or negotiations on direct links between the two sides," Shen said.

Other Chinese officials declined to clarify the proposal to open routes linking Taiwan's port of Kaohsiung with the mainland ports of Fuzhou and Xiamen, describing the deal as a reference point for the rival governments.
"These are non-government organisations," said a Ministry of Communications spokesman, referring to the negotiating bodies that forged the agreement.
"Whatever they discuss has to be used as a reference point. It is designed to give government agencies something to rely on," he told Reuters.
The spokesman would not comment on specifics of the future shipping links, such as what flags would be flown by ships operating the routes.
An official of the Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, or cabinet, also declined to comment on the accord, saying: "We have not been authorised to speak on this matter."

Taipei's chief negotiator at the Hong Kong talks was quoted by Taiwan media as saying shipping companies which had already received permission from Taiwanese authorities could now apply to China to sail directly between the island and the mainland.
China has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since the two were separated at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
Taiwan has banned direct links with China although it has allowed indirect trade, much of it through Hong Kong.
The British colony's return to Chinese rule on July 1 has pressured Taiwan to reach an understanding on direct links with its old adversary.

In Hong Kong, analysts said the territory may lose a slice of its middleman role if China and Taiwan adopt direct shipping links but the overall impact on the colony would be small, given Hong Kong's location and the sheer size of its port business.
"In 1996, we handled 13.3 million TEUs (20-foot equivalent units of containers), the highest in the world," said Richard Yuen of the Port Development Board, a government advisory body.
"We estimate that only about one million of the 13.3 million was related to Taiwan-China trade -- that was about eight percent of the total," he said.
